elements.quote: Background The following systematic review explores the uses and understandings of physical, human-to-human touch engagements in healthcare professions.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: this review sought to understand the communicative, social and affective dimensions of touches a part of healthcare, medical or nursing interventions.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the main objective.
The abstract does not specify inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: The studies were selected from five databases in March 2022.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies information sources and the date last searched.

elements.quote: underwent quality appraisal through the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to assess risk of bias.

elements.quote: presented according to the principles of thematic synthesis.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to synthesize results.

elements.quote: The synthesis produced was informed by 36 empirical studies involving either direct observation of touch practices, or recollection and discussion with healthcare professionals.
elements.reason: Reports number of studies and a brief characteristic, but does not report the number of participants.

elements.quote: We outline how medical touch has been mostly categorised as either 'instrumental' or 'expressive', with only the latter usually described as serving a communicative purpose, despite its lower incidence. We further highlight how touch seems to be operating across a fragile boundary between 'reassuring presence' and 'control', and thus requires carefulness by practitioners, and an understanding of boundaries. Then, we describe how the literature presented gender, cultural background and personal preference as elements influencing the use and perception of touch. Lastly, touch-mediated communication has been presented in some of the literature as a co-produced practice based on bodily, affective and contextual mutual attunement.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes.
No meta-analysis was conducted, as indicated by the use of thematic synthesis.
The abstract does not involve comparison of groups with effects; it is a qualitative synthesis.

elements.quote: Limitations The review could be at risk of bias given it sampled only studies written in English, French, Italian, Spanish and Finnish, thus not highlighting potentially different cultural and theoretical perspectives emerging from nonEuroAmerican contexts. Moreover, only 36% of studies included discuss patients' perspectives.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes limitations of the evidence.

elements.quote: Conclusion We argue that communication might happen in all instances of touch, while also advocating for empirical work to outline and describe the adaptive physical dynamics (e.g. changes in speed, pressure, temperature) that regulate and alter even medical procedures for communicative purposes. We also discuss the need for social scientists to radically re-conceptualise not only the theoretical scaffolding behind medical touch, but also the methodologies deployed to investigate it-advocating for a renewed attention to bodily and interactional dynamics, particularly through the deployment of (micro-)phenomenological tools, broader ethnographical engagements, or sensors for automatic recognition of bio-signals.
elements.reason: The abstract provides interpretation and implications of the results.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding.

elements.quote: While the studies in the dataset highlighted important socio-communicative dimensions of medical touch, their limited contextual variety might have obscured a certain heterogeneity one could presumably expect, given the extensive remit of the field of 'healthcare' . This is particularly cogent considering more than half of the studies summarised were conducted in one field (i.e., nursing), as well as the fact that only two studies analysed care scenarios in a non-EuroAmerican context. As far as the first element is concerned, it is important to advocate for more research on touch in different healthcare professions. It is known [105, 106] that different professional contexts and disciplines have differing caring aims: while nurses tend to provide support by coordinating patient care within medical facilities, occupational therapists work with patients often in household contexts with the ultimate aim of stimulating and facilitating functional independence, whereas physiotherapists seek to promote greater range of mobility and confidence in movement mostly through prescribed exercises.
